segments.text: A Context-Aware Analytical Framework for Quantifying the Influence of Agile Maturity on Enterprise Software Project Success Abstract-Agile practices are commonly used in the enterprise software development, however degree of how Agile maturity impacts on project success has not been quantitatively measured well; especially with reference to complex enterprise environment. Current research is primarily based on qualitative evaluations, or maturity models specific to a particular framework, which do not provide empirical evidence for how different levels of maturity relate to tangible project results. To fill this void, we present in this paper a Context- Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE)—a new interpretable analytic model intended to quantitatively appraise the influence of agile maturity on software project success and by explicitly incorporating organizationally specific contextual constraints. The approach considers Agile maturity as a multifaceted measure, extracted from major organizational and process dimensions such as teams' autonomy, the ability for continuous delivery, leadership commitment for delivering added-value to users, the integration of customer feedback into potential workflows and accumulated discipline in applying a given process. Enterprise context is defined by features like organizational size, regulatory burden, team dispersion and complexity of legacy system. Through a weighted linear estimation mechanism, CASE relates these dimensions to multi-criteria project success measures including delivery timeliness, product quality, budget-achievement performance and client satisfaction as well as realized business value. Using a dataset of an agile project from kaggle2024, the framework was empirically confirmed. The results of the experiments show projects on higher levels of agile maturity had better performance on-time 21.6%, post-release defects 17.9% and stakeholder satisfaction 24.3% than low Agile maturity projects. The overall predictive accuracy for project success was 88.7%, demonstrating that the model is robust and have practical implications. Through the provision of a transparent, context-adaptable and quantitatively-founded evaluation methodology this work provides an instrumental decision-support artefact to both small- and large-scale enterprises wanting to anchor their agile transformation endeavours towards concrete project success results. Keywords-Agile Maturity, Software Project Success, Enterprise Software Engineering, Context-Aware Analytics, Agile Performance Evaluation, Project Outcome Prediction I Introduction​ Enterprise software developers increasingly use agile development methodologies for their superior focus on flexibility, quick feedback loops, and incremental value delivery. segments.text: cross-functional cooperation have become ever more popular in complex software projects as organizations strive for faster time-to-market. On the other hand, big organizations are typically bound by regulatory demands and competing management priorities, distributed teams and governance structures of hierarchy, not to mention legacy systems that heavily impact how Agile practices can truly work. Therefore, the results of Agile adoption are quite different from one organization to another, as it is noticeable that an objective understanding was still missing about the factors of success in applying Agile practices in enterprise contexts. One of the most important factors in effective Agile is the amount an organisation has to mature within their Agile adoption. Agile maturity refers to how well Agile principles are institutionalized in teams, processes, leadership tiers and delivery methods. Although several organisations profess to adopt Agile practices, variations in maturity levels result in significantly different project outcomes such as delivery predictability, product quality, cost compliance and stakeholder satisfaction. The existing risk-guided and success-guided approaches for assessing the maturity of Agile-oriented organizations in large-scale enterprises are often qualitative, framework specific or focus on isolated dimensions that hardly support quantifying how maturity levels in turn would impact on measurable project results. To this end, this research presents a CASE, a quantitative and interpretable analytical model for quantifying how much organisational context influence in which enterprise software projects' success is achieved by Agile maturity. The proposed approach includes modelling Agile maturity as a compound index of certain organisational and process dimensions and incorporates enterprise specific situational constraints in the evaluation. This study seeks to establish the connection between maturity levels and multi-criteria project success indicators using a well-structured forecasting approach; it has the potential to create a practical decision-supporting tool for companies to properly match their Agile transformation initiatives with real-world applicable and quantifiable project success results. This research has three main contributions to the practice and academia in enterprise software engineering. First, we proposed a new CASE that quantitatively characterizes the relationship between process maturity and successful software projects, while capturing the explicit role of enterprise-specific contextual constraints. Second, the proposed approach makes Agile maturity tangible by means of synthesizing it as a composite, interpretable index which considers both organisational and process perspectives and can be used to assess systematically and replicable in heterogeneous enterprise settings. Third, we have conducted an empirical study to show that higher Agile maturity is significantly related with better levels of delivery performance in the dataset from an open source Agile project, better product quality and stakeholder satisfaction (which are all three major characteristics of

II Literature Review Junior et al. (2024) identified critical success factors (CSFs) affecting successful agile software development in a study that 25 factors were categorized by project, people, organizational, process and culture. Based on survey data and structural equation modeling, the research showed that all CSF categories have a significant effect on agile project success with projects and people being the most influential. The results highlight the interaction effect of CSFs when considered as a collective rather than individual factors [1]. Russo (2021) studied an extensive industry based case of large scale agile transformation in a mission-critical context, highlighting the importance of stakeholder commitment as key to success. An agile success model for hierarchical and plan-driven organizations was developed through post-mortem analysis and empirical validation using PLS-SEM. The findings emphasize the need for organisational levels and management acknowledgment to support agile success over long lasting transformation [2]. Khoza and Marnewick (2023) developed a theoretical model for measuring success in scaled agile, focusing on processes and perceived success factors at portfolio, program, and team levels. A correlation and regression analysis performed during the study helped to extract several success drivers at each of the three levels (e.g., strategic investment funding, ongoing exploration). The investigation highlights context-aware measurement as the missing link for facilitating the transformation agility in regulated contexts [20]. 2.1 Research Gap Many researchers have investigated Agile success factors, maturity models, leadership implications or practice patterns in different settings but with fragmented or qualitative or framework-centric views. Although existing studies have found key factors for success and suggested maturity or success models, the design of a consolidated quantitative model directly associating different Agile maturity degrees to multi-dimensional project success levels has been missing, especially in complex enterprise environments. Furthermore, contextual factors such as the size of an organization, its governance arrangement or regulatory intensity and team setting are often treated implicitly or even ignored completely which restricts the generalizability and predictability of current approaches. As a result, there are no reasonable context-aware analytical processes that can be interpreted in order to estimate empirically how such Agile maturity translates into measurable success in enterprise software projects, this leading to an open question that the present work seeks answer for. III Methodology This research uses an empirical, quantitative methodology to investigate the relationship between Agile maturity and enterprise software project performance in context based manner [21][22]. The Context-Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE) framework combines Agile maturity assessment, enterprise context modeling and multi-criteria success evaluation in a single analytic process. Agile maturity is measured in terms of a combined index obtained from vital organizational/ process dimensions [23], whereas situational constraints are reflected by observed project features. A weighted estimation model is used for modeling the relationship between maturity and the context influencing factors with project success output variables. The framework is empirically validated using Agile project data to test the predictive accuracy and sensitivity. 3.1 Research Design This paper employs quantitative, empirical research and design and it is based on secondary data from an open-source Agile project dataset [24]. A cross-sectional analytical technique is adopted to study the association of Agile maturity with enterprise contextual factors and the outcomes associated with software project success. Estimation accuracy and robustness of the proposed CASE solution are demonstrated through predictive modeling and statistical analysis. This design allows us to sensibly and systematically analyse maturity–success relations in diverse Agile

Figure 1: Architecture of the Context-Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE) Framework 3.2 Data Source and Preprocessing The open-source Agile Project Dataset (2024) is adopted as the primary data source to empirically validate the proposed CASE framework [25]. The data set contains 200 Agile software development projects, which is enough for quantitative analysis yet provides a sufficient variety of the project characteristics. We chose this dataset because it contains structured project level measures that are directly related to Agile effectiveness, management satisfaction, risk detection, efficiency and cost performance - all of which are in accordance with the fundamental aspects of Agile maturity and project success we aimed to investigate in this study. Furthermore, it is publicly available to support reproducibility and transparency that are mandatory in empirical software engineering research. Both ordinal and numerical variables have been included in the dataset. The dataset also covers several perspectives of Agile project performance. Specifically, in this study, the factors used as parameter are Agile Effectiveness, Risk Mitigation, Management Satisfaction [26], Supply Chain Improvement and Time Efficiency which are scaled using Likert scale ranging from 2 to 5; and Cost Savings in percentage (10%–48%). Project Success is encoded as a binary outcome, whether the project was completed successfully or failed. These drivers are linked to Agile maturity dimensions and multi-criteria project success criteria, in the CASE framework.

High-Level Workflow of the Proposed Context-Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE) IV Implementation Details The system is an instantiation of the CASE technology and takes a structured view-on experimental method. The dataset is randomly divided into 70% training, 30% testing for model generalization. The hybrid multi-criteria function includes six input parameters, namely; Agile Effectiveness, Risk Mitigation, Management Satisfaction, Time Efficiency and Cost Savings in addition to the binary Project Success. These factors are applied to calculate the index Agile maturity, contextualized adjustment factors and multicriteria project success score. The model is calibrated on the training sample through ordinary least squares regression, allowing us to easily estimate how Agile Maturity and situational factors influence success. The CASE model corresponds with the top-right corner of the plot, which delivers 21.6% higher improvement in on-time delivery and 88.7% in prediction accuracy than any of the comparisons. This finding demonstrates the utility of combining Agile maturity assessment with enterprise context modeling to strengthen both operational results and reliability for success estimation in enterprise Agile projects. 5.1 Ablation Study To evaluate the contribution of individual components within the proposed CASE framework, an ablation study was conducted by selectively removing key modeling elements. The analysis examines the impact of excluding enterprise context adjustment, Agile maturity weighting, and multi-criteria success aggregation on overall prediction performance. The results demonstrate that each component contributes significantly to the effectiveness of the CASE model, with the full configuration achieving the highest performance. Table 3. The conclusion is that combined Agile maturity assessment, contextual adaptation and multi-criteria success assessment are required to provide robust and reliable estimation of project success. 5.2 Discussion​ The experimental results show that the proposed Context-Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE) can predict an agile success text better than all other respondents

The concluded improvements in on-time delivery, defect elimination and stakeholders’ satisfaction showed that it is possible to achieve concrete project gains when maturity level of Agile Toward all those findings are added the enterprise context consideration.These results support our argument that a higher agile maturity translate into tangible project benefits. Comparative examination discloses that conventional models not only tend to concentrate on process adoption or individual success factors but also do not take into consideration contextual barriers that impact effectiveness of Agile in large-scale context. Moreover, the ablation study demonstrates that enterprise context information modeling is the most critical and its removal results in the-deepest decrease in prediction accuracy. Combined, these results justify the need for an integrated and context specific, quantitative based framework to provide a reliable measure of success for enterprise level Agile projects. VI Conclusion​ In this work we presented the Context-Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE), a model that is quantitative and interpretable for assessing the impact of Agile maturity on enterprise software project success. The proposed model combines Agile maturity assessment and enterprise context modeling with multi criteria success evaluation, combining factors for estimating the outcomes of a project in a complex organization. Experimental results indicate that, CASE gains 21.6% improvement in on-time delivery, reduces post-release defects by 17.9%,enhances stakeholder satisfaction by 24.3%,and in addition has a high accuracy of predicting project success at 88.7% compared with existing models of agile maturity andsuccess.. Notwithstanding the positive findings, some limitations related to using a single public source dataset and proxy-contextual variables. Future work will involve validating the framework on various enterprise datasets, long-term analysis and further extent of CASE with non-linear and learning-based estimation methods.
